front: What four challenges drove the SunOS kernel redesign described by Eykholt?
back:
• Symmetric multiprocessing
  • Multithreaded applications
  • Real-time
  • Multimedia
Applied to the SunOS/SVR4 kernel.

text: The kernel was restructured around {{c1::threads}}, which are used for most asynchronous processing, including {{c2::interrupts}}.

front: According to the Abstract, what two properties does restructuring the kernel around threads give the result?
back: It is fully preemptible and capable of real-time response. The lecture notes never say the kernel is preemptible.

front: What did the team explicitly want to go further than, rather than settle for?
back: "Merely adding locks to the kernel and keeping the user process model unchanged."

front: State the first design goal regarding threads of control per user process.
back: Multiple threads of control per user process, each able to execute system calls and handle page faults independently, and able to run concurrently on different processors on an MP. The user-visible thread architecture is in [Powell 1991].

front: What was the second design goal, and what does achieving it require?
back: Bounded dispatch latency for real-time threads [Khanna 1992]. It requires absolute control over scheduling, hence preemption at almost any point in the kernel and elimination of unbounded priority inversions wherever possible.

front: What is the paper's rationale for giving the kernel a thread facility like the one offered to applications?
back: The kernel is itself a complex multithreaded program, so it benefits from a thread facility essentially the same as the one offered to user applications for managing multiple asynchronous activities.

front: What system is the result of this redesign, and what are its four headline features?
back: The SunOS 5.0 kernel, core OS component of Solaris 2.0: fully preemptible, real-time scheduling, symmetric MP support, and user-level multithreading. Several locking strategies were described earlier in [Kleiman 1992].

front: What is the fundamental entity scheduled and dispatched onto a CPU, and how heavy is it?
back: The kernel thread. It is "very lightweight": only a small data structure and a stack.

front: Why is switching between kernel threads relatively inexpensive, and how does this differ from the notes?
back: Switching between kernel threads never requires changing virtual memory address space information. The notes make this point only for threads of the same user process, not for kernel threads in general.

front: Why do kernel threads form a fully preemptible, real-time "nucleus" inside the kernel?
back: Kernel threads are fully preemptible and can be scheduled by any scheduling class, including the real-time (fixed-priority) class; because all other execution entities are built on kernel threads, they form a fully preemptible, real-time nucleus.

front: In the Overview, what determines a thread's priority under the synchronization protocols, and what notes topic does this introduce?
back: Primitives support protocols that prevent priority inversion, so a thread's priority is determined both by the service it performs and by which activities it is impeding by holding locks [Khanna 1992]. The P2 notes never mention priority inversion or priority inheritance; the P3L1 scheduling note later covers priority inversion and boosting the mutex owner's priority.

front: What asynchronous kernel work is done by kernel threads, and what three benefits does this bring?
back: Asynchronous disk writes, servicing STREAMS queues, and callouts. Benefits: removes "diversions" in the idle loop and trap code; increases concurrency (other CPUs can do the work); gives each asynchronous activity its own priority for scheduling.

text: Eykholt states that all LWPs have a kernel thread, but {{c1::not all kernel threads have an LWP}} (e.g. system threads, interrupt threads).
extra: The notes only describe kernel threads that back LWPs.

front: What are the two stated motivations for separating user threads from LWPs?
back:
• The user library [Stein 1992] can switch user threads quickly without entering the kernel
  • A process can have thousands of user threads without overwhelming kernel resources

front: In traditional UNIX, where did kernel per-process and processor data live?
back: All kernel per-process data lived in the user and proc structures; processor data in global variables. Per-process data split into non-swappable data in proc and swappable data in user; the swappable kernel stack was allocated with the user structure in the user area, usually one or two pages long.

front: How does the restructured kernel split its data?
back: Three ways: per-LWP-and-kernel-thread, per-process, and per-processor.

front: What happened to the user structure in the restructured kernel?
back: The proc structure keeps a "vestigial" user structure, now much smaller than a page and no longer practical to swap.

front: What does the LWP structure hold, and what do the notes omit?
back: The process control block (pcb) for user-level processor registers, plus system call arguments, signal masks, resource usage, profiling pointers, and pointers to its kernel thread and its proc. The notes omit profiling pointers, the pcb term, and the back-pointers.

front: Where is the LWP's kernel stack allocated?
back: Together with the LWP structure, inside a swappable area.

front: What fields does the kernel thread structure hold, and what do the notes understate?
back: Kernel registers, scheduling class, dispatch queue links, and pointers to the stack and the associated LWP, process, and CPU structures. The notes say only "scheduling info" for the scheduling class and dispatch queue links.

front: Why does the thread structure also hold some LWP data?
back: Because the thread structure is not swapped, it holds some LWP data needed even while the LWP structure is swapped out.

front: What does the cpu structure hold, and how portable is it?
back: Pointers to the currently executing thread and that CPU's idle thread, plus current dispatching and interrupt-handling information. It has an architecture-dependent substructure; the main body is meant to fit most MP architectures.

front: On SPARC, how is the current thread structure accessed in a single instruction?
back: A dedicated register, global register %g7, points to the current thread structure; the C macro curthread gives single-instruction access to its fields. Current LWP, proc, and CPU are reached through pointers in the thread structure. Additional global registers may later be dedicated to other hot structures.

front: What three scheduling classes does SunOS 5.0 support, and what does a class do?
back: System, timesharing, and real-time (fixed-priority). A class determines relative priority within the class and converts it to a global priority.

text: With multithreading, scheduling classes and the dispatcher operate on {{c1::threads}} instead of {{c2::processes}}.

front: Which thread does the dispatcher run, and how are ties broken?
back: The thread with the greatest global priority; threads of equal priority are dispatched round-robin.

front: Why was the kernel made preemptible, and how limited is preemption disabling?
back: To better support the real-time class and interrupt threads. Preemption is disabled only in a small number of bounded code sections, so a runnable thread runs as soon as practical after its priority becomes high enough.

front: What does running thread A do when it releases a lock on which higher-priority thread B sleeps?
back: A immediately puts itself back on the run queue and lets the CPU run B.

front: On an MP, what happens when A outranks B but B outranks the current thread on another CPU?
back: That CPU is directed to preempt its current thread and choose the best thread. The notes describe only the user-library analogue (signalling another KLT).

front: What can user code running on a sufficiently high-priority kernel thread do?
back: User code on a kernel thread of sufficient priority (e.g. real-time) executes even while lower-priority kernel threads wait for CPU. Details in [Khanna 1992].

front: What scheduling class do system threads usually belong to, and how are they scheduled?
back: They usually belong to the system scheduling class and are scheduled like any other thread; they can be created for short- or long-term kernel activities.

front: Why and how are a system thread's thread structure and stack allocated?
back: System threads need no LWP, so their thread structure and stack are allocated together in a non-swappable area.

front: What is the seg_kp segment driver, and how do system threads vs LWPs use it?
back: It handles stack allocation: kernel virtual memory that can be paged or swapped out, with "red zones" against stack overflow. System threads use it for stack and thread structure in a non-swappable region; LWPs use it for the LWP structure and kernel stack in a swappable region. The notes mention red zones only for user-level thread stacks.

front: What four synchronization objects does the kernel implement internally, and what do the notes omit?
back: Mutexes, condition variables, counting semaphores, and multiple-readers/single-writer (readers/writer) locks [Powell 1991]. The P2 notes cover mutexes, CVs, and the readers/writer problem built from them; semaphores and reader/writer locks as primitives come only in P3L4.

front: When and how is a synchronization object's behavior specified?
back: When it is initialized (type plus optional type-specific argument). Operations take a pointer to the object and may behave differently depending on that type.

front: How can synchronization-object statistics be enabled?
back: Most object types can collect statistics such as blocking counts or times. A patchable kernel variable can make the default types statistics-gathering, so stats can be enabled per object or kernel-wide.

front: What determines how a primitive impedes progress (sleep, spin, etc.)?
back: It is a function of initialization; by default, primitives that can logically block may sleep.

front: Which synchronization primitives get priority inheritance, and which do not?
back: Supported only for strictly bracketing primitives (locker must be unlocker) with a single determinable owner: mutexes and rw locks held for writing. Semaphores, CVs, and read-held rw locks do not get it [Khanna 1992].

front: How do signal-interruptible wait variants (e.g. cv_wait_sig(), sema_p_sig()) behave on a pending signal?
back: The primitive returns a value saying it was interrupted, and the caller must release resources and return. There is no non-local jump to the head of the system call as with the traditional sleep routine.

front: Besides the object pointer, what do all of Eykholt's kernel synchronization init calls (mutex_init, rw_init, sema_init) take?
back: A name string, a type, and a type-specific argument.

front: In Eykholt's kernel synchronization interfaces, what do the try variants (e.g. mutex_tryenter, sema_tryp) and signal variants (e.g. cv_wait_sig, sema_p_sig) return?
back: An int status.

front: Which kernel condition-variable call in Eykholt's Figure 4 provides a timed wait?
back: int cv_timedwait(cvp, lp, long tim).

front: In Eykholt's kernel readers/writer lock API, what do rw_downgrade and rw_tryupgrade do, and which can fail?
back: rw_downgrade converts a writer to a reader. rw_tryupgrade converts a reader to a writer and may fail (it returns int).

front: What extra argument does sema_init take compared with the other kernel synchronization init calls?
back: An initial value (unsigned int val), in addition to the name string, type, and type-specific argument.

front: Why do kernel synchronization primitive types use names like kmutex_t and kcondvar_t?
back: They use different names from the user ones (kmutex_t, kcondvar_t, krwlock_t, ksema_t) so applications that read internal kernel data structures do not confuse them.

front: What is the most heavily used kernel synchronization primitive, and what is its purpose?
back: Mutexes, which prevent races on shared data, are by far the most heavily used primitive.

front: For how long are mutexes meant to be held?
back: For short intervals; e.g. a critical system mutex should not be held while waiting for disk I/O.

front: What two rules does the mutex implementation enforce, and why?
back: Mutexes are not recursive (the owner cannot call mutex_enter() again on the same lock), and the thread that holds a mutex must be the one to release it. Enforced to promote good practice and avoid deadlocks.

front: When mutex_enter finds the lock set, what determines the blocking action?
back: The type passed to mutex_init and stored in the mutex.

front: What is the default adaptive mutex policy (type MUTEX_DEFAULT)?
back: It spins by polling the owner's status while the owner (recorded at acquisition) remains running on a processor, and sleeps once the owner stops running. This gives fast response and low overhead for simple contention.

front: What does MUTEX_SPIN take as its argument, and why is it rarely used?
back: Its argument is the interrupt level to disable while the mutex is held. It is rarely used because adaptive mutexes are generally more efficient.

front: What must device drivers use, and how does MUTEX_DRIVER decide spin vs adaptive?
back: Device drivers must use MUTEX_DRIVER, whose argument is a Sun-DDI-defined opaque value (essentially an interrupt priority). It selects spin if that priority is above the "thread level", adaptive otherwise.

front: What is the fast-path trick that makes mutex_enter() try the adaptive lock first?
back: Non-adaptive mutexes use a separate primitive lock field, and the field the adaptive type uses is kept permanently locked. So mutex_enter() always tries the adaptive lock first and considers other types only if that fails.

front: Why is a synchronization object's queue header not stored in the object itself?
back: Every object needs a way to find threads suspended on it, but many system structures embed synchronization objects, so their storage cost must stay small; the queue header is therefore not stored in the object.
source: Turnstiles vs Queues in Synchronization Objects

front: What do the two bytes in a synchronization object locate, and what does it contain?
back: They locate a turnstile structure containing the sleep queue header and the priority inheritance information [Khanna 1992]. The notes say nothing about turnstiles.
source: Turnstiles vs Queues in Synchronization Objects

front: What is guaranteed about the number of preallocated turnstiles?
back: Turnstiles are preallocated so there are always more turnstiles than active threads.
source: Turnstiles vs Queues in Synchronization Objects

front: What alternative to turnstiles was rejected, and why were turnstiles preferred?
back: Rejected: choose a sleep queue from an array by hashing the object's address (what traditional sleep() did). Turnstiles were preferred for more predictable real-time behavior, since a turnstile is never shared with other locks, whereas hashed sleep queues sometimes are.
source: Turnstiles vs Queues in Synchronization Objects

front: How did other MP kernels (Ultrix, multithreaded SVR4) handle synchronization primitives?
back: They had several synchronization primitives with the same semantics (e.g. mutual exclusion) that explicitly either sleep or spin [Hamilton 1988], [Peacock 1992].

front: With spin mutexes shared with interrupt handlers, what must happen around acquisition, and how do the notes frame it?
back: The interrupt priority level must be raised before acquiring and lowered after releasing, high enough to keep out any handler that uses the object, else deadlock. The notes describe this as masking a signal/interrupt, not raising the interrupt priority level.

front: What is drawback 1 of spin mutexes shared with interrupt handlers?
back: Raising and lowering interrupt priority can be expensive, especially on architectures with external interrupt controllers, and mutexes are heavily used.

front: What is drawback 2 of spin mutexes shared with interrupt handlers (modular kernel)?
back: Subsystems are interdependent and interrupt-handler requests (e.g. mapping kernel memory, memory allocation) can touch many subsystems. So many subsystems' mutexes must protect themselves at relatively high priority, keeping interrupt priority high for long periods and imposing the raise/lower cost on every acquire/release.

front: What is drawback 3 of spin mutexes shared with interrupt handlers?
back: Interrupt handlers must live in a constrained environment that avoids any kernel function that might sleep, even briefly.

front: How does SunOS 5.0 treat most interrupts, and how does this differ from the notes?
back: It treats most interrupts (not all) as asynchronously created and dispatched high-priority threads, which may sleep and use the standard primitives. The lecture presents it as universal (the note's Paper callout adds the exception) and does not mention their priority.

front: How does the kernel protect the act of putting threads to sleep from interrupts?
back: It uses a primitive spin lock protected by raised priority, one of the few bounded sections where interrupts are locked out. Traditional UNIX ([Leffler 1989], [Bach 1986]) also protects the dispatcher by locking out interrupts, usually all of them.

front: What is the "thread level", and how are interrupts above it handled?
back: A modifiable threshold: interrupts above it are not handled as threads and are treated like non-portable "firmware" (e.g. simulating DMA via programmed I/O). These handlers can synchronize only via spin mutexes and software interrupts.

front: In traditional UNIX (and earlier SunOS), how were interrupts handled relative to the interrupted process?
back: The interrupted process is held captive (pinned) until the interrupt returns; handlers run on the interrupted process's kernel stack or a separate interrupt stack; the handler must finish and get off the stack before anything else runs on that processor; the kernel synchronizes with handlers by blocking interrupts in critical sections.

front: Why does SunOS 5.0 preallocate interrupt threads, and what does it do on an interrupt?
back: A full thread creation per interrupt is impractical, so it preallocates interrupt threads that are already partly initialized. On an interrupt it does the minimum work to move onto the interrupt thread's stack and make it the current thread.

front: Immediately after moving onto the interrupt thread, how are the two threads related?
back: They are not fully separated: the interrupt thread is not yet a full-fledged thread (cannot be descheduled), and the interrupted thread is pinned until the interrupt thread returns or blocks and cannot proceed on another CPU. On return, the interrupted thread's state is restored.

front: Can interrupt threads nest?
back: Yes; an interrupt thread can itself be interrupted and pinned by another interrupt thread.

front: What is "passivation", and when is most of the full-thread cost paid?
back: If the interrupt thread blocks on a synchronization variable (mutex or CV), it saves state ("passivates") to become a full thread runnable on any CPU, then control returns to the pinned thread. Most of the full-thread cost is paid only when it must block due to contention.

front: On SPARC, what does passivation cost include, and when is it incurred?
back: Flushing the entire register file; done only if the handler sleeps, not during uncontended handling.

front: While an interrupt thread is in progress or blocked, what happens to its level and lower interrupts, and why?
back: Its level and all lower-priority interrupts are blocked by the normal priority mechanism. If it blocks they stay disabled, because the handler may not be reentrant at the block point or may still be doing high-priority work that lower-priority work must not interrupt.

front: Where does a blocked interrupt thread stay bound, and why?
back: It stays bound to the CPU it started on, as an implementation convenience and to guarantee an interrupt thread is always available when an interrupt occurs (the authors note this may change).

front: How does the cpu structure track that an interrupt at a level has blocked?
back: A flag records that an interrupt at that level has blocked, and the minimum interrupt level is noted. Whenever the interrupt level changes, the CPU's base interrupt level is checked, and the actual priority level is never allowed below it.

front: What does release_interrupt() do?
back: It lets an interrupt thread continue as a normal high-priority thread: it saves the pinned thread's state and clears the blocked indication, letting the CPU lower its interrupt priority level.

front: What are the instruction counts for interrupts as threads, and what caveat do the notes omit?
back: About 40 extra SPARC instructions per interrupt taken versus about 12 saved on the mutex enter/exit path. The net gain holds only as long as interrupts do not block too frequently; the notes give the numbers but not this caveat.

front: Describe the memory cost of preallocated interrupt threads (per-level, per-CPU, SPARC numbers).
back: One interrupt thread is preallocated per potentially active interrupt level below thread level, per CPU, plus one system-wide interrupt thread for the clock. SPARC has nine interrupt levels that can use threads. Each thread needs a stack and data structure, roughly 8 KB, so memory cost can be high.

front: How could the interrupt-thread memory cost be reduced with a smaller pool?
back: Since all levels are unlikely to be active at once, a smaller per-CPU pool could be used, blocking all further below-thread-level interrupts when the pool is empty, capping simultaneous active interrupts.

front: How often does the clock interrupt fire on Sun SPARC?
back: 100 times per second.

front: How many clock interrupt threads are there system-wide, and when is the clock thread invoked?
back: A single clock interrupt thread for the whole system, not one per CPU; the clock handler invokes it only if it is not already active.

front: How does the clock thread handle being delayed more than one tick?
back: It can be delayed more than one tick by blocking on a mutex or by higher-level interrupts. If a tick arrives while it is active, the interrupt is cleared and a counter incremented; before returning, the clock thread checks the counter, decrements it, and repeats clock processing.

front: What locking approach does the kernel use almost exclusively, and what is the invariant?
back: Data-based locking: each mutex and rw lock protects a set of shared data, as opposed to protecting routines (monitors). Every piece of shared data is protected by some synchronization object.

front: Which locking topics were covered in [Kleiman 1992], and which does this paper elaborate on?
back: VM, file system, STREAMS, and device driver locking were in [Kleiman 1992]. This paper elaborates only on device drivers, because they are closely tied to interrupt threads.

front: What is an MT-unsafe driver?
back: A driver not modified to protect itself against concurrency (no locking of its own).

front: What interim mechanism serializes MT-unsafe drivers?
back: Wrappers acquire a single global mutex, unsafe_driver, so only one MT-unsafe driver is active at a time.

front: Through what paths can drivers be entered, and what must each do if unsafe?
back: Explicit entry points, interrupts, and call-backs; each entry must acquire unsafe_driver if the driver is unsafe. Example: when an MT-unsafe driver uses timeout(), the callout structure is marked so unsafe_driver is held during the later function call.

front: How does old sleep() interact with unsafe_driver?
back: MT-unsafe drivers may still use old sleep()/wakeup(). sleep() releases unsafe_driver after the thread is asleep and reacquires it before returning.

front: How is the longjmp() feature of sleep() preserved for unsafe drivers?
back: If a thread sleeping with a dispatch value greater than PZERO is signalled, it longjmps to a setjmp() done in the unsafe-driver entry wrapper, which returns EINTR to the driver's caller.

front: What safety check does sleep() perform on its caller?
back: It checks that its caller is an MT-unsafe driver and panics otherwise; it is unsafe to use from a driver that does its own locking.

front: What are MT-safe and "MT-hot" drivers?
back: Simple locking is easy to add, so almost all drivers have some of their own; those are called MT-safe regardless of granularity. "MT-hot" is used by some developers for drivers with fine-grained locking.

front: Instead of an a-priori lock hierarchy, what tool did the team build, and what does it do?
back: locknest, a lint-like static analysis tool that reads C source, builds call graphs, and reports locking cycles (lock-ordering violations).

front: What benefit do the authors credit locknest with, and what similar tool is cited?
back: It helped early implementation debugging and probably reduced time spent debugging deadlocks. A similar tool, Sema, is described in [Korty 1989].

front: What is the side benefit of priority inheritance for deadlocks?
back: Deadlocks from hierarchy violations are usually detected at run time too.

front: For which locks does run-time deadlock detection work well, and where does it fail?
back: Works well for mutexes and write-held rw locks, but cannot always find deadlocks involving read-held rw locks because there is no complete list of reader threads. Condition-variable deadlocks are not detected.

front: What was the SVR4 Multiprocessor DDI/DKI, and what locking model did it use?
back: UNIX International and USL were defining the SVR4 Multiprocessor DDI/DKI (Device Driver Interface / Driver-Kernel Interface) with a different set of locking primitives based on the traditional interrupt-blocking model.

front: How does SunOS 5.0 support the SVR4/MP DKI primitives?
back: It implements those interfaces, to the extent then defined, on top of its own locking primitives and ignores any spin semantics, so such drivers port easily. Native SunOS drivers normally use SunOS primitives.

front: How does kernel time slicing work, and what does it enable even on a uniprocessor?
back: Because the kernel is fully preemptible, code was added to the clock interrupt handler to preempt whatever thread it interrupted, making kernel threads time-slice. This gives nearly arbitrary code interleavings even on a uniprocessor.

front: What did raising the clock interrupt rate accomplish, and why did time slicing stay useful after MP hardware existed?
back: It made time slicing more effective at exposing windows where data was unprotected, finding locking bugs on uniprocessor hardware before MP hardware existed; it remained useful afterward because uniprocessors far outnumbered multiprocessors.

front: Why is kernel time slicing intended only as a debugging feature?
back: Because it has some, though slight, performance cost.

front: According to the Summary, what are the primary features of SunOS 5.0?
back:
• Fully preemptible real-time kernel
  • High concurrency on SMPs
  • User thread support
  • Interrupts handled as independent threads
  • Adaptive mutexes
It is a multithreaded, symmetric MP version of the SVR4 kernel.

front: How does the Summary describe the relationship between kernel and user-level thread models?
back: They are almost identical: scheduling kernel threads onto CPUs is analogous to the library scheduling user threads onto LWPs.

front: What costs does the Summary note from structuring the kernel with threads?
back: Threads have "mostly good effects" but can be overused. Costs: stacks are large and must be on separate pages if stack-overrun protection is wanted; context switching is still expensive.

front: What does the Summary say is still sometimes better than threads?
back: Some things are still better implemented with callouts and other "zero-weight" processes, though threads are a good structuring paradigm for the kernel.

front: The notes and lecture call the kernel thread's stack swappable without qualification. What is the paper's actual position?
back: Only LWP-backed threads have a swappable kernel stack (allocated with the LWP); system threads' stacks and thread structures are non-swappable. The notes and lecture describe Figure 2 (a user process), where the claim holds; they just leave out system threads.

front: How many LWPs can a kernel thread have, per Eykholt et al.?
back: A kernel thread has at most one associated LWP, and system and interrupt threads have none. The lecture says "the associated LWP" (singular), and illumos (kthread_t's single t_lwp) agrees.
